plan.contextChunk: This figure lines up three panels, labeled (a), (b), and (c), that carry a matching problem in a bipartite graph over into a flow network. Panels (a) and (b) draw the same graph as two vertical columns of unlabeled gray circles, five in the left column beneath the italic L and four in the right column beneath R, joined by thin straight edges that always cross from one column to the other and never link two circles within a column. In (a), two edges are thickened with a gray band behind them, and no circle is an endpoint of more than one of them. In (b), three edges carry that same gray band, still with no shared endpoints, so one further circle on each side is now covered. Panel (c) redraws the arrangement with direction: a circle labeled s stands left of the L column and fans arrows into it, every L-to-R edge becomes a rightward arrow, and the R circles send arrows into a circle labeled t at the far right. The gray band in (c) traces three vertex-disjoint routes running from s all the way through to t. Holding the shaded arrows of (c) against the shaded edges of (b) is the comparison the panels invite, and together they set up the construction in which a maximum flow of unit-capacity edges delivers a matching of the largest possible cardinality.

interactionPlan.concept: A bipartite matching of any size corresponds one-to-one with that many vertex-disjoint unit flows from s to t in the associated flow network, so a maximum flow yields a maximum matching.
elements: panel (a): bipartite graph with left column L of 5 gray circular nodes and right column R of 4 gray circular nodes
thin black edges in (a) connecting L nodes to R nodes (no edges within a column)
2 gray-thickened matching edges in (a) with no shared endpoints
panel (b): identical bipartite graph with 3 gray-thickened matching edges, still endpoint-disjoint
panel (c): flow network with source node s at left, the L column, the R column, and sink node t at right
directed arrows s→L for every L node in (c)
directed arrows L→R matching the bipartite edges in (c)
directed arrows R→t for every R node in (c)
3 gray-thickened directed paths in (c) tracing vertex-disjoint routes from s through L and R to t
italic labels L and R beneath the two columns in each panel
node labels s and t in panel (c)
panel captions (a), (b), (c)

interactions.label: Panel
interactions.teaches: Increasing the matching by one edge corresponds to adding exactly one more vertex-disjoint s-to-t route in the flow network — matching cardinality and flow value are the same number
Clicking one shaded s-to-t route in panel (c) lights up its full path and simultaneously highlights the corresponding L-R edge in the matching, revealing that one unit of flow IS one matched pair

interactions.label: Augment matching
interactions.teaches: Each augmentation finds one route from an unmatched L node to an unmatched R node (an augmenting path) and raises the matching size by exactly one, mirroring how augmenting flow raises flow value

demo_steps.title: A small matching
demo_steps.narration: Panel (a) shows a bipartite graph with two shaded matching edges — no node touches more than one shaded edge, so this is a matching of size 2.

demo_steps.title: Augment to size 3
demo_steps.narration: Press Augment: one more edge is shaded, covering one additional node on each side. The matching grows from 2 to 3 along a single augmenting path — the largest matching this graph admits.

demo_steps.title: Same problem as a flow network
demo_steps.narration: Panel (c) adds source s and sink t with all edges directed rightward. The three shaded routes from s to t are vertex-disjoint and carry exactly the matching of panel (b).

demo_steps.title: One flow unit = one matched pair
demo_steps.narration: Click any shaded s-to-t route: the whole path lights up and its middle L-R edge is the matching edge. Flow value 3 and matching size 3 are the same quantity in two languages.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Every unit of s-to-t flow passes through exactly one L-R edge, so an integral max flow in the unit-capacity network is literally a maximum matching — flow value equals matching size.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Three side-by-side panels with the same node geometry so switching feels like a transformation, not a new picture. Left column L has 5 evenly spaced light-gray circles, right column R has 4, offset so edges cross between columns at varied angles. Matching edges drawn as a thick semi-transparent gray band behind the thin black edge line. Panel (c) keeps the L and R columns in the same relative positions, adds s to the left of L and t to the right of R (labeled in italic serif), arrowheads on all edges pointing right, and three gray-banded vertex-disjoint routes s→L→R→t. When a route is clicked, tint it a distinct highlight color (e.g. warm orange) and flash the matching edge in panel (b)'s geometry. Show one panel at a time per the toggle, with captions (a), (b), (c).

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between panels (a), (b), and (c): the display switches from a size-2 matching to a size-3 matching to the flow network, making clear how increasing matching cardinality corresponds to adding one more disjoint route.
- Click for a shaded s-to-t route in panel (c): the full path lights up and the matching edge between L and R is highlighted in panel (b), making clear that one unit of flow represents one matched pair.
- Button for stepping through augmentation: each press adds or redirects one shaded edge until three endpoints are matched on each side, making clear how an augmenting route raises the matching size.

authoredContext: The maximum-bipartite-matching problem Given an undirected graph G D .V; E/, a matching is a subset of edges M _x0012_ E such that for all vertices _x0017_ 2 V , at most one edge of M is incident on _x0017_. We say that a vertex _x0017_ 2 V is matched by the matching M if some edge in M is incident on _x0017_; otherwise, _x0017_ is unmatched. A maximum matching is a matching of maximum cardinality, that is, a matching M such that for any matching M0 , we have jMj _x0015_ jM0 j. In this section, we shall restrict our attention to finding maximum matchings in bipartite graphs: graphs in which the vertex set can be partitioned into V D L [ R, where L and R are disjoint and all edges in E go between L and R. We further assume that every vertex in V has at least one incident edge. Figure 26.8 illustrates the notion of a matching in a bipartite graph. The problem of finding a maximum matching in a bipartite graph has many practical applications. As an example, we might consider matching a set L of machines with a set R of tasks to be performed simultaneously. We take the presence of edge .u; _x0017_/ in E to mean that a particular machine u 2 L is capable of performing a particular task _x0017_ 2 R. A maximum matching provides work for as many machines as possible. Finding a maximum bipartite matching We can use the Ford-Fulkerson method to find a maximum matching in an undirected bipartite graph G D .V; E/ in time polynomial in jV j and jEj. The trick is to construct a flow network in which flows correspond to matchings, as shown in Figure 26.8(c).

discrepancies: The source presents all three panels (a), (b), (c) side by side in one composite; the generated figure shows only one panel at a time behind a radio toggle, so the at-a-glance comparison of matching growth and the flow-network reduction is lost in the default state
In panel (c) the shaded flow-route bands are drawn on top of the directed edges and can partially cover the L→R arrowheads, slightly obscuring the edge directions the source keeps crisp
The source's thick matching bands sit flush under the node circles; minor, but the rounded line-cap bands here slightly overshoot the node rims
evaluation.notes: Node positions, the 7-edge bipartite graph, both matchings, and the directed s–t flow network are all faithfully reproduced with correct shaded bands, and the panel toggle, augment animation, step player, and clickable flow routes are pedagogically strong; the main cost is that the three-panel side-by-side composition of the source is hidden behind a toggle.
action_items: Draw the shaded route bands in panel (c) before (under) the directed edge lines and arrowheads so arrows stay fully visible
Use 'butt' line caps and shorten bands by the node radius so the gray matching bands terminate cleanly at node rims
Consider a combined 'all panels' view or making the radio toggle more visually prominent so users immediately discover panels (b) and (c)

feedback.rationale: All scores are 4–5 with an overall average of 4.8, zero failure modes, and verification passing; the remaining issues are minor polish (band layering, line caps) and a deliberate toggle design choice, so further iteration risks diminishing returns.
